types.AA: Follow the rim all the way around. Later craters can bite into an older rim, and deposits on the floor can partly bury it. Where two rims cross, the one that cuts the other formed later.
types.AL: The landmark was mapped by the light it reflects. Trace the change in brightness from orbit, then move in to see which ridges, plains or craters cross that boundary. A single marking can cover several kinds of terrain.
types.AR: The mapped outline bends into an arc. Following both ends helps distinguish the sweep of the whole feature from shorter marks crossing it.
types.CA: A sequence of crater rims traces a line across the surface. Compare the spacing of the depressions and see where neighboring rims overlap. A chain alone does not establish whether all its craters formed in one event.
types.CB: Look for steep-sided hollows with irregular outlines. From above, the intervening strips of higher ground make it easier to separate individual depressions in a group.
types.CH: The ground breaks into pieces with different orientations. Trace the edge of an intact block and compare it with the jumbled terrain between blocks.
types.CM: Follow the canyon along its length, then look across it. The opposing walls reveal its width, while offsets and branches show how far the system continues beyond a single viewpoint.
types.CO: These small hills are easiest to distinguish under low sunlight. Their individual shadows help separate neighboring summits that look like a single patch from overhead.
types.CR: An oval outline encloses terrain with a different pattern inside it. Trace the rim, then compare the ridges that run along it with those that cut across it.
types.DO: The line on the map follows high ground. On an oblique approach, look for the crest and the slopes falling away on either side.
types.ER: This label marks a center of volcanic activity on Io. Lava and plume deposits can change the surface between spacecraft visits, so the date of an observation matters here.
types.FA: Look for a patch that stands out because it reflects more light than its surroundings. Its boundary can differ from the outline of any landform beneath it.
types.FE: A low ridge follows a scalloped course across Europa's ice. From overhead, follow successive bends and look for places where another surface marking cuts across them.
types.FL: Trace the edge of the flow-shaped terrain. Where one lobe overlaps another, their outlines can preserve the order in which material reached the surface.
types.FM: This channel on Titan is a possible route for liquid hydrocarbons. Following it downslope can reveal how branches join and where a channel meets a lake or sea.
types.FO: The long depression is easiest to pick out across its width. A line of shadow along one wall can give the impression of a ridge until the opposite wall comes into view.
types.FR: These broad, round edifices on Venus have unusually flat tops. Look for a steep break at the margin, the feature that gives them their informal name of pancake domes.
types.FT: This narrow passage joins larger bodies of liquid on Titan. Follow the shores on either side to see where the passage widens into open water.
types.IN: Here land breaks the surface of a Titan sea or lake. Its shoreline gives radar mappers an outline to follow even when the interior terrain has little contrast.
types.LA: A mass of material moved downslope here. Look uphill for the place it broke away and downhill for the wider deposit where the slide came to rest.
types.LB: Intersecting ridges or valleys divide this terrain into a maze. Pull back until several branches are visible to see why a single valley view misses the larger pattern.
types.LC: The name identifies a small plain with a distinct outline. The Latin word for lake has different meanings on different worlds.
types.LF: Astronauts used names like this to find their way and record where observations and samples came from. The scale of the landmark can be much smaller than a crater visible from Earth.
types.LG: Look beyond the center for a pattern of surrounding rings. The outer arcs can survive well beyond the point where the central structure stops resembling an ordinary bowl.
types.LI: A long marking can be traced by its contrast with adjacent terrain. At intersections, look for which marking continues uninterrupted and which one it crosses.
types.LN: This projection of a plateau has a rounded, tongue-like outline. Follow its margin back toward the higher ground to see how it joins the main plateau.
types.LU: The outline resembles a dry lake bed on Titan. Cassini mapped many such depressions as well as lakes that still held liquid.
types.MA: The name picks out a dark patch. Comparing its outline with the surrounding relief helps distinguish a change of surface material from a shadow cast by high ground.
types.ME: The broad, darker area is easiest to trace from high above the surface. Early observers borrowed the word for a sea to describe markings visible in a telescope.
types.MN: A relatively flat summit ends at steep sides. Try tracing the upper edge from above before descending beside the scarp.
types.MO: The label identifies mountainous terrain. Compare its footprint from orbit with its profile from the side. The catalog measures its horizontal extent, while summit elevation is a separate measurement.
types.OC: The dark expanse stands out even in a small telescope. On the Moon these lowlands preserve the record of lava spreading over older terrain.
types.PA: The traditional name marks a small plain. Follow its margins to see where smoother ground gives way to more rugged terrain.
types.PE: Trace the irregular rim of this depression. A scalloped outline or several overlapping hollows can make a patera look very different from a simple circular bowl.
types.PL: This is low-lying terrain. The transition to higher ground at its edges is often easier to see on a shallow approach than from directly overhead.
types.PM: A broad stretch of elevated ground forms a plateau. The break in slope at its margins is a better guide to its shape than color alone.
types.PR: This headland projects from higher ground. Look for the change of outline where it juts into the surrounding lunar plain.
types.PU: Voyager 2 saw dark material carried aloft above Triton's bright southern surface. Winds bent the plumes and carried fine material downwind, leaving long streaks on the ice.
types.RE: This name covers a region large enough to contain smaller named features. Zoom out to trace the broad color or terrain pattern that gives the region its identity.
types.RI: A narrow rille cuts across the lunar surface. Trace its course to see whether it curves, runs straight or branches. Rilles with different shapes can have different origins.
types.RU: Follow the break in elevation along this scarp. Low sunlight picks out the face, while an overhead view reveals the length and curvature of the edge.
types.SC: A steep edge follows a lobed or irregular course across the terrain. Looking along it gives a different sense of its scale from looking straight down at its outline.
types.SE: This winding feature changes character along its length. Some stretches stand above the adjacent ground and others lie below it.
types.SF: The letter identifies a separately mapped lunar feature associated with a nearby named landmark. It gives observers a way to distinguish several features in the same neighborhood.
types.SI: A bay-like outline indents the edge of a larger plain. Trace the two sides from the mouth inward to see the shape that gave rise to the name.
types.ST: This point records a spacecraft landing. Its position ties observations made on the ground to features visible from orbit.
types.SU: A series of furrows and ridges runs across the surface. Follow several side by side to see where they curve together or give way to an older pattern.
types.TA: The name spans a broad tract of land. Smaller features within the region are useful landmarks when the whole named area no longer fits in view.
types.TE: Crossing sets of ridges and troughs break the ground into a tile-like pattern. Radar images of Venus reveal this structure through the planet's opaque clouds.
types.TH: A rounded hill or small mountain rises above the surrounding ground. Its summit and the outline of its base are easiest to distinguish from different viewing angles.
types.UN: Repeated dune crests record the action of wind on loose grains. Follow the crests across the field and look for places where they bend around obstacles.
types.VA: Trace the valley from one end to the other and look for tributaries or changes in width. The shape can preserve clues to how material once moved along it.
types.VI: The streak is defined by its contrast with adjacent terrain. Its direction and continuity across other markings are useful clues when comparing maps of Titan.
types.VS: The plain stretches beyond the scale of an individual crater or ridge. An orbital view shows its extent, while a low pass reveals the smaller landforms that interrupt it.

199: MESSENGER mapped Mercury from orbit. The planet preserves both ancient impact scars and long cliffs formed as its interior cooled and the crust contracted.
299: Magellan mapped Venus by transmitting radar through the clouds. A bright return can come from rough terrain or a slope facing the instrument, so a radar image and an elevation map answer different questions.
301: On the Moon, low sunlight brings out relief along the day-night boundary. Under a high Sun, shadows shrink and differences between bright ejecta, dark basalt and older highland material stand out.
401: Phobos is so irregular that a single impact can change its silhouette. Its low gravity and dusty surface make the surroundings of a crater quite different from those of an equally wide crater on Mars.
402: Spacecraft images show a smoother surface on Deimos than on its neighbor Phobos. Loose material has partly filled some depressions, softening crater outlines that might otherwise be clear.
499: Wind can move loose material across Mars today. Orbital topography helps separate changes in the shape of the ground from changes in its coating of bright dust or dark sand.
501: Repeated tidal flexing supplies heat to Io. Eruptions cover old surfaces with fresh material, so comparing observations from different spacecraft can reveal changes on human timescales.
502: Europa's water-ice shell retains many intersecting ridges and relatively few impact craters. Where an older line ends against a younger one, their intersection can reveal the local sequence of events.
503: Ganymede preserves two conspicuous kinds of terrain. Darker regions carry many old craters, while brighter regions are often grooved. Their boundaries record episodes when the icy crust was reworked.
504: Callisto's densely cratered surface preserves a long impact record. Clean ice exposed by some impacts stands out against darker surroundings, making differences in surface material visible from orbit.
601: Craters cover much of tiny Mimas. Their sizes and abundance vary from place to place, giving scientists a way to compare the histories of different parts of the icy surface.
602: Cassini found that Enceladus combines old cratered areas with much younger fractured terrain. The south polar fractures feed jets of water vapor and ice grains from a moon with an ocean beneath its shell.
603: Water ice makes up much of Tethys. Over geological time it can deform under its own weight, muting the relief of very large impact structures while parts of their outlines survive.
604: Dione's bright wisps puzzled observers until Cassini saw them up close. Some are faces of ice cliffs in systems of fractures that cut across older cratered terrain.
605: Rhea's surface is ice-rich and heavily cratered. Where a small crater interrupts the rim of a larger one, their overlap records which impact happened later.
606: Cassini's radar could look through Titan's haze. It revealed landscapes shaped by flowing liquid, dune fields and polar seas on a world cold enough for methane and ethane to play roles water plays on Earth.
608: Iapetus presents two very different hemispheres. Dark material absorbs more sunlight, while colder, brighter terrain can retain water ice. That difference helps sustain one of the strongest color contrasts among Saturn's moons.
701: Voyager 2 photographed part of Ariel during its 1986 flyby. Broad valleys cutting cratered terrain reveal that the surface continued to change after many of its impacts.
702: Umbriel is the darkest of Uranus's large moons. Voyager 2 photographed a heavily cratered surface in 1986, but the encounter provided much more detail on the illuminated hemisphere than on the one in darkness.
703: Voyager 2 found long fault valleys on Titania. Their crossing directions indicate that the crust was pulled apart. Ice exposed along some valley walls reflects light more strongly than the surrounding terrain.
704: Oberon's impacts expose contrasts between bright rays and dark deposits on some crater floors. Voyager 2 supplied the close views during its 1986 encounter with Uranus.
705: Miranda's surface juxtaposes old cratered ground with regions of sharply patterned ridges and valleys. The abrupt boundaries were among the most surprising discoveries of the Voyager 2 encounter.
801: Voyager 2 recorded active plumes when it passed Triton in 1989. Ices and dark windblown streaks share the landscape with ridged areas nicknamed cantaloupe terrain.
901: New Horizons saw deep fractures and a contrast between rougher northern terrain and smoother southern plains on Charon. These differences preserve evidence of changes within the crust of Pluto's largest moon.
999: New Horizons found that different ices play different roles on Pluto. Water ice can support mountains, while softer nitrogen ice can flow as glaciers across low ground.

overrides.301:ME: The dark floor is basalt. Ancient lava flooded parts of the lunar lowlands and cooled into broad plains. Follow the boundary with the brighter highlands to see where the lava stopped or left high ground exposed.
overrides.301:LC: Early lunar cartographers gave small dark plains the names of lakes. Look along the edge for the contrast between the smoother floor and the brighter, more rugged highlands.
overrides.301:SI: Lunar cartographers used the word for a bay where a dark plain extends into the brighter highlands. The curving edge often reveals more of the topography than the nearly uniform floor.
overrides.301:AA: Compare the rim with the craters that interrupt it. A smaller crater cut into the rim must be younger. Low sunlight brings out terraces, central peaks or a simple bowl, depending on the size and preservation of the crater.
overrides.606:ME: Titan's polar seas hold liquid hydrocarbons. Cassini's radar could map their shores through the haze because smooth liquid usually returns little of the transmitted radar signal.
overrides.606:LC: Cassini's radar mapped small, sharply bounded lake features through Titan's haze. Where liquid is present, methane and ethane can remain liquid in the extreme cold at the surface.
overrides.606:SI: This inlet lies along a hydrocarbon shoreline. On Cassini radar maps the usually dark liquid outlines the headlands, so a bay can be followed even through Titan's thick haze.
overrides.606:AL: Titan's haze hides its surface at visible wavelengths. Infrared observations can pick out broad light and dark markings underneath. Radar maps give a different view of the relief and roughness within the same region.
overrides.499:AL: Observers mapped this marking through telescopes long before spacecraft could measure the heights beneath it. Dust cover can change its visibility. A brightness map and an elevation map can therefore show quite different boundaries here.
overrides.499:AA: An impact excavated this part of Mars. Inspect the rim and floor separately. Windblown deposits can collect inside an old crater while its raised rim remains visible for much longer.
overrides.502:LI: Long lines cross Europa's water-ice shell. Some resolve into paired ridges with a groove between them. At an intersection, the line that cuts across the other helps establish which part of the icy surface changed more recently.
overrides.502:CH: Here Europa's ice shell has broken into blocks. Some retain stripes that no longer line up with the terrain around them, evidence that pieces shifted before the intervening material solidified.
overrides.299:AA: Magellan mapped Venus through its clouds by radar. Look for the crater rim and its surrounding ejecta. Radar brightness depends on roughness and viewing geometry, so a bright patch alone does not measure height.
overrides.299:CR: On Venus a corona can have a belt of ridges and fractures around its margin. These structures are studied for what they can reveal about hot material rising beneath the crust.
overrides.705:CR: Miranda's coronae are enormous patterned regions of ridges and troughs. Following their borders reveals how abruptly these terrains meet the moon's more heavily cratered landscapes.
overrides.501:PE: Many volcanic depressions on Io contain lava flows. Hot material registers strongly in infrared observations, while a cooled crust can hide molten lava beneath it.
overrides.503:SU: Grooved terrain is characteristic of Ganymede. Parallel ridges and troughs record extension of the icy crust. Look for the boundary where the grooves meet darker cratered ground.
overrides.604:CM: From a distance these features helped give Dione its wispy appearance. Cassini resolved great fractures and bright ice cliffs that cut across the older cratered surface.
overrides.504:CA: Chains of craters are common on Callisto. One explanation is a comet breaking into fragments before impact. A line of separate bowls is the observation that such an explanation has to account for.
